text.text: You are considering ending an employee's employment. This is the highest-stakes management decision you will make and carries significant legal exposure if not handled correctly.

• An employee who failed to meet goals outlined in a formal Performance Improvement Plan.
• Someone who violated a zero-tolerance policy (harassment, theft, falsifying records).
• A long-tenured employee whose role is being eliminated as part of a restructuring.
• An employee who has received multiple written warnings and continues the same behavior.
• Someone whose conduct in a single incident was severe enough to warrant immediate termination.
• An employee who abandoned their position without notice or explanation.
• A manager whose team filed multiple substantiated complaints about their leadership.
• Someone who failed a drug or background screening that is a condition of employment.
Gather and preserve these records as you work through the check.

1. Compile the full disciplinary history in chronological order: verbal warnings, written warnings, PIP, and outcomes.
2. Confirm in writing that the employee received, signed, and had a chance to respond to each step.
3. Document the specific reason for termination in one clear sentence — this will appear in official records.
4. Note the date HR and/or legal reviewed and cleared the termination.
5. Prepare a separation checklist: final pay, equipment return, benefit end dates, COBRA notice, access revocation.

elements.text: You can attach files and links securely from the completed assessment before submitting it to HR.

text.text: Watch for: Any termination where the employee recently filed a complaint, requested accommodation, took protected leave, or belongs to a protected class.
Contact HR: Contact HR before scheduling the meeting, before saying anything to the employee, and before preparing any paperwork. No termination should move forward without HR sign-off.
